single prominent agent, often referred to as the host, interacts with multiple less prominent agents, referred to as guests, who have contrasting opinions on a particular topic.  The host aims to gather the most informative opinions from the guests through targeted query selection.  Unlike other active learning settings, the host is unaware of the guests' individual identities and opinions.  The host can only access a collective opinion that is a weighted sum of the guests' opinions, based on voting weights.  The host's primary goal is to minimize the uncertainty about a target product by allocating limited query budget to the collective of guests.  The author proposes a formal framework for modeling this scenario and presents an efficient algorithm known as FRER for computing the optimal allocation and query targets.  The author analytically shows that FRER achieves a level of performance that is comparable to the optimal allocation when the optimal query targets are known.  Additionally, the author presents an expanded version of the algorithm that tackles the uncertainty about the target product by applying a broader set of query operators.  The results of thorough experiments conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in comparing the opinions of multiple experts.

(LISA) will provide highly accurate measurements of gravitational waves in the frequency range of 0.001-0.1 Hz, enabling insights into highly informative gravitational wave signals produced by supermassive black hole mergers. LISA data will offer unique signatures in the gravitational wave spectrum, such as quasiperiodic oscillations resulting from interactions between black holes and the surrounding accretion disks, and potential dark energy imprint. Additionally, LISA will be capable of detecting the gravitational wave background produced by numerous merging black hole and neutron star systems. However, instrumental noise generated by LISA's frequency fluctuations will obscure these indirect indicators of black hole mergers. This study explores possible methods for extracting valuable information about black hole mergers from the background produced by LISA's frequency noise. We analyze various techniques such as the Fourier time-domain method, the Fourier frequency-domain method, and the time-domain method, and find that the latter yields the most accurate results. Using future LISA data simulations, we anticipate that this method will enable the determination of black hole mass functions involving both massive black holes and stellar-mass black holes within a 10% margin of error. Furthermore, we anticipate that this method will allow for the determination of quadratic mass-distance power laws in massive black hole mergers and quadratic mass power laws in stellar-mass black hole mergers within a 25% margin of error.

These models are trained on a dataset that includes both the measured data and the theoretical equations in which the physical constants appear.  They are then able to make predictions on previously unobserved data sets, including new measurements and unknown physical phenomena.  However, it is crucial to assess the credibility of these predictions, taking into account the uncertainties inherent to the measurement process.  This can be achieved by treating the measurement uncertainties as perturbations in the theoretical equations, from which we derive a set of stochastic differential equations that describe the behavior of the physical constants.  These equations form the basis for constructing a stochastic operator that enables us to evaluate the uncertainties of the physical constants directly.  We demonstrate this approach using a simple example involving the Schr\"{o}dinger equation and further apply it to a more complex scenario of neutrino oscillations, incorporating genuine measurement uncertainties.  Our method provides a way to quantify the uncertainties of all physical constants within these theories and novel phenomena predicted by them, obtaining a concrete number from an infinite range.

Utilizing this strategy, our results show that it's feasible to obtain reliable estimates of the complexity of Lexicon-semantic verb phrases with just a handful of singularly informative configurations out of an exponentially large set of possible interpretations.  These findings form the basis for an efficient hybrid approach combining both static and dynamic analysis methods.  By generating sets of possible interpretations for each verb phrase through runtime evaluation and identifying the most singularly informative configurations among them, our hybrid system provides a precise and reliable assessment of its complexity.

isy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, are hindered by programming challenges and limited qubit numbers.  A promising approach to overcome these limitations is through quantum chemistry simulations that utilize entangled states to mimic chemical compounds.  A recently developed protocol, known as full-field adiabatic passage, offers an alternative to complicated programming. This paper explores the optimal use of EH technology in a two-node cooperative communication system with one of the nodes capable of harvesting energy from the surrounding environment. Neural Networks and Monte Carlo Tree Search, have seen significant growth in the field of machine learning.  By leveraging multiple neural networks to make decisions, they have been shown to improve predictive performance and stability.  Despite their success, traditional methods like Bayesian Neural Networks are computationally expensive and demand extensive technical expertise.  In contrast, the proposed SimpleSwap Ensemble (SSE) is a cutting-edge framework that is both cost-effective and accessible.  SSE introduces a novel ensemble framework based on a straightforward exponential scoring system, where network predictions are weighted according to their confidence levels.  This results in enhanced performance, as demonstrated by our findings, alongside a significant reduction in training time.  SSE's user-friendly design makes it an appealing option for practitioners looking to implement neural network ensembles with minimal technical overhead.

neural network architectures in an unsupervised manner for the task of image classification. Initially, we investigate how to leverage existing classification knowledge to guide the design of efficient networks through an unsupervised pruning strategy, focusing on capacitive reduction. We introduce UNITE, a method utilizing knowledge that enables both the identification of superfluous connections and the grouping of functional parameters. UNITE demonstrates superior performance compared to leading supervised and unsupervised methods in the design of efficient neural networks. Furthermore, we showcase the versatility of UNITE by applying it to the Mobilenetv3 benchmark, a more recent and challenging benchmark. rising computational capacities, artificial neural networks have grown larger and more complex. As a result, real-world optimization tasks for these models are now frequently limited by numerical stability constraints rather than computational ones. Professional optimization libraries have responded by adopting double-precision floating point arithmetic, which has led to a rise in efficient neural network designs that minimize excessive memory usage. We believe current design paradigms based on precision are temporary and will become irrelevant as researchers better understand the effects of reduced precision on neural network performance. As a first step towards this understanding, we were studying the influence of memory storage on neural network behavior when we came across an intuitive yet unexplored idea - that memory usage in neural networks is ultimately determined by their signal-to-noise ratio. We developed a theoretical framework based on this concept and applied it to create novel neural network architectures such as DenseConnect and DensePrune, which achieved state-of-the-art performance in various image classification tasks while requiring significantly less model parameter count. Our findings demonstrate that memory storage has a direct proportional relationship with the noise level in neural networks, and we were able to further establish that the noise level has a direct cubic relationship with the width of the network. We are sharing our code and models for the DenseConnect Large dataset and DensePrune with 1.3 million parameters, and achieved 75.16% top five accuracy on the ImageNet validation set.

field models with multiple symmetry breakings to understand how chiral fermion effective interactions change within the context of a particular symmetry breaking pattern known as "spontaneous symmetry breaking in stages" (SSBIS). Two key concepts in these models are the scalar sector and the fermion sector. The scalar sector is made up of complex self-interacting scalar fields that break symmetry in stages, while the fermion effective interactions depend on the scalar sector. Our analysis begins by considering an empty vacuum state where both left- and right-handed fermions can be massless. We then determine the fermion mass matrices in each stage of symmetry breaking and find that they are proportional to the corresponding scalar potential. To support our findings, we present numerical data for a specific particular stage of symmetry breaking. Additionally, we explore the general case of more than one fermion type and confirm that the (symmetry breaking stage-dependent) fermion mass ratio remains constant. This is based on an analytical expression derived from the Weyl fermion mass matrix eigenvalues.

Although there have been proposals to overcome this limit by leveraging magnetic materials with low energy content, a more thorough investigation is needed into the fundamental limitations of energy consumption in stochastic computing.  In this work, we establish a tighter bound on the energy required for computing, taking into account the inherent randomness in physical systems.  Our analysis reveals that achieving ultimate energy efficiency in computing would necessitate a setup with an exponentially low energy cost, where information is represented through the resistance change of massive parallel circuits consisting of fundamental magnetic units.  A concrete scheme based on spin torque oscillators is presented as a viable means of realizing this bound, although with a significant gap in terms of energy efficiency in current technological standards.

various fields like computer science and robotics, and a particular task known as object recognition in images aims to identify a single class of objects within a single image.  Object recognition in videos, on the other hand, involves detecting a single class of objects consistently across multiple frames in a video.  A specific task called one-shot object recognition in videos demands identifying a single object class both in static images and in videos, with the added challenge that the model must treat these scenarios as related.  A related task known as few-shot object recognition in videos requires models to recognize new object classes either in images or videos, with the added difficulty that the model must consider its prior knowledge of other object classes.  A task known as object recognition in videos across different views demands identifying objects consistently across various camera perspectives, with related tasks included in views like object recognition in videos from front-facing cameras and recognition in images from any camera angle.  Other related tasks are object recognition in videos with different lighting conditions, object recognition in rotating videos, and object recognition in videos of moving objects.  A task known as object recognition under transformations demands identifying objects consistently across various transformations, with related tasks included in object recognition in videos of rotating objects and recognition in videos of moving objects.  A meta-task known as the robustness ladder involves making the model more resilient to various transformations by repeatedly applying them, with a related sub-task included in the robustness ladder's object recognition component. By combining ab initio structural optimization, phonon calculations and Bertschinger functional, this study investigates local atomic arrangements within HfO$_{\rm x}$ layers on the surface of the Hf(110) substrate.  The results show that these layers can be found in an epitaxial rock-salt structure with some vacancies, and that their stability is rooted in the minimized strain energy present when the lattice constant is set to 4.24 ${\rm \mathring{A}}$.  Theoretical models of lattice vibrations, or phonons, reveal that certain high-frequency modes are consistent with those found in other rock-salt compounds, and that some lower-frequency modes are unique to this system and indicative of bond changes between atoms.  By employing the Bertschinger functional to model these vibrations, this research demonstrates that the unique arrangements of atoms within the HfO$_{\rm x}$ layer are a result of the interplay between strain and the varying oxygen content.  Consequently, this may explain previous experimental observations of delayed lattice relaxation and oxygen non-stoichiometry in this system.

the human brain remains an area of ongoing research. Certain brain disorders, particularly those affecting the cerebral cortex, have been linked to alterations in the Wright society structure. The Wright society is a theoretical model comprising interconnected modules that form a large, highly ordered grid. Researchers have developed the Wright Society Network (WSN) to create ordered cortical networks based on spatially organized modules. Studies utilizing the WSN have found that certain brain disorders result from disrupted inter-module relationships rather than changes within individual modules. Furthermore, a recent discovery indicates that the Wright Society may also be applicable to the study of gene regulation within the brain. Genomic analysis reveals that certain genes involved in neurodegenerative disorders exhibit similar patterns of co-expression with the Wright Society. Specifically, researchers found that the protein products of these genes are involved in similar biological processes and are often part of the same complex. Interestingly, the Wright Society was able to predict relationships between these genes even when they were not explicitly connected. This suggests that the Wright Society may be a useful tool for identifying additional genes involved in neurodegenerative disorders and other brain disorders.

However, the hard exponential space of actions for connected roads presents a significant challenge.  To address this issue, many experts represent the driving map as a grid, restricting movements to their perceived optimum.  This approach restricts the potential movements of the vehicle to a limited set of roads.  Instead of constraining the possible movements, our proposed method, called Exponential Action Space for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (EAS-MARL), aims to optimize the driving map efficiently.  EAS-MARL trains an autonomous vehicle agent to decide on the most beneficial course of action across the entire network of roads through direct experience.  This method enables the generation of safe and efficient driving paths.  Comparisons of EAS-MARL to traditional MARL methods, such as multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradients (MDDPG), reveal that EAS-MARL produces better driving results.

This exciton reactivity makes them ideal for studying non-lithographic physics and potential applications in quantum processing.  However, excitons in free space dissipate quickly due to their inherent instability.  Trapping these excitons within a parabolic potential well, generated by laser coupling to a nearby semiconductor, results in stable, long-lived quasiparticles that can be localized in any desired area.  Using a numerical model based on the microscopic equations for semiconductor interband processes, we simulate the creation of exciton traps and demonstrate their utilization in constructing quantum islands and barriers.  We also investigate the effects of linearity vs. nonlinearity in laser-semiconductor interactions on trap formation and show that nonlinear processes produce a more efficient, long-lasting trap.

(GNNs) are particularly effective in labeling graph-structured data with arbitrary labels.  However, their capability to generate natural language descriptions of graph data surpasses many specialized models, including those designed for network visualization.  This disparity prompts researchers to investigate the limit of GNN-based text generation.  To this end, we introduce the Novel Description Benchmark (NDB), a novel evaluation metric that assesses the innovativeness of generated descriptive text relative to existing graph data.  Our experiments demonstrate that beyond basic accuracy, GNN-based text generators fall short in producing novel descriptions.  This shortfall is attributed to several factors, including the tendency of GNNs to prioritize central graph nodes over others and the reliance on nearest neighbors that impedes innovation.  Our findings also suggest that the novelty of generated descriptions is often outweighed by noise introduced by GNNs.  As a result, users may find the generated descriptions either repetitive or unrelated to the actual graph data.  To address these limitations, we propose several strategies to refine the novelty of generated descriptions and observed these refinements to enhance the novelty score while maintaining descriptive accuracy.

Furthermore, by examining a less stringent condition (i.e., when the jet can be modeled as having a linear density gradient), we are able to compare our results to previous, inexact approaches to this problem.  Consequently, this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between the physical characteristics of jets of active galactic nuclei and the distinctive spectral features that emerge from the relativistic electrons within these jets.

The application of quantum phase locking is demonstrated for the largest-scale optical systems observed to date, involving the synchronization of light waves in the 10 petahertz range. The entanglement of the two-photon states is measured by analyzing the correlation between the photons and the quantum states of the optical systems. The results show good agreement with theoretical models and reveal the formation of entangled two-photon states even in the highest frequency range studied. The occurrence of entanglement in these systems can be comprehensively understood by considering the frequency detunings of the cavities and the rates at which quantum nonlinearity occurs. The optimal generation of entangled two-photon states is achieved through careful selection of system parameters based on a correlation function that quantifies the relationship between the photons. The potential of these systems to generate multi-photon entanglement and the application of quantum phases locking to produce complex quantum states of light are also discussed. The optical systems used in this study are based on highly integrated quantum photonic multi-cavity systems consisting of quantum dots acting as both photon sources and nonlinear devices. The system operates under strong light confinement within microcavity structures with nominal dimensions measuring only 1,000 times the wavelength of the light. The tight confinement of light within these systems enhances the rates of quantum nonlinearity by several orders of magnitude, effectively making them more suitable for the generation of multi-photon entanglement.

A recent study discovered that in a one-shot, anonymous public goods game, approximately 60% of participants prioritize contributing to the group over personal gain, providing a potentially positive outlook for cooperation. However, when players are positioned to benefit from others' contributions, a significantly lower proportion of around 20% exhibit cooperative behavior, which might be seen as surprisingly low when compared to the first scenario. This paper delves deeper into understanding this disparity by examining various decision-making processes that lead to cooperative behavior in the two social dilemmas presented. It appears that contributing to the group is primarily driven by a spontaneous, impulsive tendency, whereas the more enduring, persistent tendency is more strongly linked to the second dilemma. Additionally, differences in cooperative behavior were found across gender lines, with females exhibiting the spontaneous, impulsive tendency and males displaying the persistent, impulsive tendency.

Developing an efficient and practical reliability measure method is crucial for analyzing the resilience of road networks.  We investigate alternative graph reliability measures including edge-disjoint cuts, closest points, and shortest paths.  Focusing on the smallest cut set (SCS) method, we develop an efficient formula for calculating the reliability of a single edge.  Furthermore, we present different strategies for selecting sets of edge-disjoint cuts and provide a detailed case study using the Texas transportation network.  Our analysis compares and contrasts various SCS methods including the minimum cut set method.  Investigating closest point reliability, we introduce the concept of a unidirectional closest point set (UCPS) which provides a more precise reliability calculation for an individual edge compared to the strongest path set (SPS).  In addition, we introduce the closest point set (CPS) method for determining the reliability of a single network edge.  Our research provides several practical applications for network reliability analysis including the evaluation of a single road segment, the assessment of a snow removal operation, and the calculation of the reliability of an individual bridge.

This time, we examine the corresponding question for the linear wave equation in space-time domains divided into non-uniform grids. By direct analysis of the difference scheme's operator, we establish conditions under which the linear wave equation's solutions converge as the grid size approaches zero. This involves demonstrating the existence of an equivalent difference scheme operator that converges at a rate of O(h^2), where h represents the grid size. The exact timing and relationship between the development of magnetic structures and these particle release events remains poorly understood. A specific type of magnetic reconstruction, potential field model coronal field models, are commonly used to depict the configuration of magnetic structures. These models are known to accurately depict quasi-static structures such as solar arcades, but may not capture the intricate details of impulsive phenomena. SSNs generate an internal representation of the scene by utilizing a single sampled object point.  They do this by producing an encoded scene representation (ISR) for any viewing angle, making them applicable to various rotation-invariant applications such as object categorization.  An extended version of SSNs, called the generalized self-supervised scene network (GSSN), has been developed for tasks that prioritize scene understanding over object identification.  GSSNs split the scene representation into disjoint parts corresponding to individual objects within the scene.  Each part is responsible for describing a single object's characteristics. An end-to-end learning version of both SSNs and GSSNs has been created, incorporating a mechanism for generating object masks. Experimental results using the ModelNet40 dataset have shown GSSNs to excel over traditional object-based methods in rotation-based binning tasks.

an infectious individual over their infectious period is referred to as the basic reproduction number (R0) in epidemiological models.  We present a novel expression for R0, specifically tailored for models featuring nonlinear contact transmission and varying population mixing, and investigate its maximum value within a well-mixed environment.  Analyzing the expression, we find that it takes a particularly straightforward form when modeling homogeneous populations, reducing to a simple fractional product that reflects the characteristics of the infectious disease over time.  Conversely, in a heterogeneous population, the expression becomes more complex, incorporating factors that consider the host's epidemiological status.  Through mathematical approximation, we derive an effective R0 estimate by averaging the fractional product from the T-segment of the epi-curve, and demonstrate that it aligns with existing first-generation discretized SIR models, yielding an average that typically falls short of the critical R0 threshold of one by a significant margin.  Notably, this result holds despite the recent outbreak-driven shift towards more contagious variants.  We further speculate that the prevailing decline in R0 may be attributed to an unforeseen consequence of transmission homogenization, where the rising risk posed by minor variations in transmission probability exerts downward pressure on R0.  Ultimately, our research offers a fundamental R0 expression that can be utilized for any infectious disease, along with a novel insight that may underpin the accelerating decline in transmission probabilities observed in recent times.

phrase often used to contrast two entities that are very different.  Research on this idiom has primarily focused on its literal and figurative interpretations, without exploring its fundamental nature as a metaphorical expression.  This study reverses this approach by examining the underlying structure of "like night and day" as a composite idiom composed of two distinct components, night and day.  Through corpus analysis and elicitation techniques, we uncover new insights into this phrase.  A key finding reveals that "like night and day" is used more frequently than expected to indicate a small degree of difference, contrary to its typical association with significant contrasts.  Another significant discovery indicates that this idiom is more closely related to "night and day" in terms of duration than we initially assumed, with people perceiving a difference of one day as a notable gap.  Furthermore, our results show that the direction of this idiom, whether beginning with night or day, influences its meaning, suggesting that the contrast is relative to the speaker.  Overall, this research demonstrates the value of investigating idioms as integrated units, rather than breaking them down into individual parts.

A key finding reveals that the extension of continuous functions between $(0,1)$-metric spaces is continuous, where this continuous result applies to functions between subspaces of positive real numbers equipped with their standard metric.  This discovery extends a previous result from S. Dovdanov, providing a solution to the problem he posed.  Additionally, our research explores extensions of continuous functions between general $(0,1)$-metric spaces and identifies specific requirements for these extensions to be continuous.  A new concept, the density of a $(0,1)$-metric space, is introduced and shown to play a crucial role in determining the continuity of function extensions.  Further study focuses on the topological properties of dense $(0,1)$-metric spaces and the behavior of functions within these spaces.  Key aspects of dense spaces include their ability to sustain a compatible topology equivalent to that of the real numbers and the existence of sequences with unique limit points in these spaces.  The results obtained also recognize the connection between dense spaces and spaces with the property of being chainable, a concept first introduced by M. Matviashenko.  This research expands the criteria previously established for chainable spaces, providing additional requirements that involve the density of these spaces.  Finally, the paper addresses questions related to the compactness of subsets within dense spaces and the behavior of functions at the boundary points.

Utilizing a statistical approach based on symmetrized mean-field models, we establish a range of possible reactions within a maximum entropy framework. This approach is further refined by incorporating a chemical potential related to symmetry, which drives symmetry-sensitive reactions until equilibrium is reached among all involved species. By comparing our results to recent gamma-ray burst (GRB) observations, we attempt to correlate the production of high-density symmetries with the energy released in these reactions, specifically in terms of $e^+/\gamma$. Our analysis indicates that the highest $e^+/\gamma$ ratios, exceeding 10%, could be produced in a narrow energy range ($\approx 0.04$ $10^{51}$ erg) associated with moderate-latitude GRB observations. This suggests that the high-density symmetry approach could account for the enriched gamma-ray bursts often linked with narrow GRB photospheres.

ontologies being publicly available, many domains still remain uncovered or are only partially defined.  This issue can be addressed by incorporating existing overlapping knowledge from various ontology sources.  This paper presents the PilotSystem, an automatic ontology construction tool designed to integrate information from multiple source ontologies within a particular domain.  PilotSystem takes in a set of source ontologies along with their class hierarchies, maps concepts to their respective ontological classes, and utilizes this classification to merge the source ontologies based on their hierarchical relationships.  The resulting integrated ontology comprises a generalized hierarchy of all the original ontologies' classes, with each specific instance corresponding to a distinct original ontology.  For example, consider using PilotSystem to integrate ontologies of animals, birds, and eagles.  The resulting integrated ontology would contain a single 'eagle' class that's a subcategory of both 'animals' and 'birds'.

2 viral transmission is primarily through respiratory droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, or talk. Understanding the underlying physics of droplet propagation is essential to analyzing the spread of the virus. In this study, we investigate how voice affects the movement of aerosolized droplets by comparing two scenarios: one influenced by voice and the other silent. Using high-speed imaging and advanced image processing techniques, we analyze the position, velocity, and acceleration of droplets in both scenarios. Our findings reveal that voice significantly impacts droplet behavior, with the majority being expelled at a maximum velocity of approximately 5.5 m/s. However, some droplets reach distances up to 2.5 times farther than those that did not interact with voice. Our data also shows that droplets typically experience maximum deceleration due to gravity, but in the presence of voice, their acceleration and velocity patterns change, indicating an increased tendency to linger in the air.

Language Processing and Computer Vision, the creation of unified models capable of handling both visual and language inputs has become increasingly feasible.  While existing models typically focus on single-task applications, a small subset of these models have been developed with the ability to handle both visual and language inputs, and are thus particularly suited for tasks such as visual question-answering and captioning.  A more recent model, the one presented by Li et al., has demonstrated excellence in multiple visual and language tasks, sparking curiosity about its internal workings.  Through application of various analysis techniques, including activation mapping and pruning, we have gained valuable insights into this model's behavior, uncovering surprising aspects of how it processes information.  For example, we discovered that the residual connection within the attention mechanism has a significant impact on the model's visual transformer block, enabling it to learn highly effective representations.  Conversely, we found that the visual transformer block's ability to learn global image understandings is actually hindered when the connection is present.  We have also found evidence supporting the claim that the visual transformer block is primarily responsible for learning object knowledge, while the language-based cross-attention mechanism learns more about the sentence's content.  We have publicly shared the tools used for these analyses, and hope that they can serve as a useful resource for the entire community.

This survey aimed to explore medical students' opinions on learning from electronic health records as part of their curriculum. ic Extrapolation (CE) for solving complex systems of equations that arise from the Monte Carlo finite element approximation of elliptic PDEs. Monte Carlo methods involve solving complex systems of equations of the form $Ax = b$ where $x$ represents randomised nodal values, typically involving large matrices $A$ with dimensions in the billions. Our work specifically addresses these large-scale systems with approximately 10,000,000,000 degrees of freedom. We examine the performance of CE in several settings, including when the Monte Carlo approximation is precise and when there is significant error. Our results show CE offers significant speed improvements over traditional iterative methods like Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient when the Monte Carlo approximation is precise, achieving a speed-up of over 5 times. However, when the Monte Carlo approximation introduces significant error, CE requires significantly more iterations, ultimately performing similarly to traditional iterative methods. Notably, our findings also suggest CE can effectively reduce the computational cost per iteration by half when the Monte Carlo approximation is not precise. We illustrate the efficacy of CE in real-world scenarios using two Monte Carlo finite element simulations, demonstrating it is an efficient algorithm for solving large-scale complex systems of equations that arise from the Monte Carlo approximation of elliptic PDEs.

While prior research examined the effects of collaborative programming on learning outcomes and discovered some collaborative benefits, it left unanswered questions concerning the specific roles of collaboration in learning.  To investigate this further, 30 pairs of students were asked to complete various programming tasks either alone or with a partner.  The results showed that collaborative programming yielded superior outcomes when challenges were moderate, but alone-based programming performed better when difficulties were high or low.  Additionally, an assessment revealed that students who shared the work equally experienced the most beneficial outcomes when tasks were complex.  In contrast, students who collaborated but didn't divide the work fairly struggled with difficult tasks and enjoyed little benefit.  Interestingly, students who took on separate tasks during collaborative programming did not necessarily learn more than those who worked together on integrated tasks despite any potential benefits.  Thus, equal sharing of work seems crucial when students collaborate on challenging programming tasks.

coming decade will be to pinpoint the composition of dark matter and dark energy through surveys of the cosmos.  Next-generation spectroscopic surveys on fibers will confront the "fiber collision effect," a limitation on the number of objects that can be measured simultaneously, which will impact their dark matter and dark energy findings.  We develop a statistical model that accounts for the fiber collision effect in the measurement variance to determine the optimal fiber layout for maximizing simultaneous measurements while minimizing variance, and this can be achieved efficiently despite the restrictive packing limits.  Compared to a naive random sampling approach, using our optimal layout leads to a 3.5 times improvement in the number of simultaneous measurements, a 30% reduction in variance, and a 50% reduction in the variance of dark matter and dark energy estimates, which will significantly enhance the cosmological measurements of these surveys.

of a spin-coated polymer film as it transitions from a randomly dispersed state to a highly ordered mesophase. This transition is facilitated by heating the film to its glass temperature and then slowly cooling it. The random distribution of molecules gives rise to an amorphous state, characterized by paired correlation functions that reflect the lack of long-range order. As the film undergoes a glass transition and is slowly cooled, the amorphous state persists, with a pair correlation function that indicates a disordered arrangement that persists over a distance of approximately 10-100 nanometers. In contrast, the highly ordered mesophase emerges when the film is heated to its glass temperature and then slowly cooled, either directly or indirectly, allowing the molecules to align over a distance of up to several hundred nanometers. We observe this large-scale order to be unstable, however, and susceptible to disruption by inserting another type of polymer into the film. The random polymer acts as defects within the film, breaking up the large-scale ordered regions, although it has a minimal effect on the smaller-scale amorphous state. The size of the large-scale ordered regions varies depending on the specific type of polymer used, with some films displaying larger areas of order than others, and can be influenced by changing aspects of the film's composition.

Coulomb barrier presents significant challenges for both experimental and theoretical assessments.  Experiments involving alpha-induced reactions on light targets are particularly complicated to measure accurately due to the dense spectra produced, which result from the high recoil energies experienced by the target nuclei.  As a consequence, determining absolute cross-sections for these experiments is an intricate task, which necessitates employing sophisticated spectroscopic analysis to extract useful information on energy levels and transition probabilities in the involved nuclei.  In this review, our primary focus is on a comprehensive examination of available data, including previously unanalyzed spectra, in order to revisit and reevaluate existing information on energy levels and transition probabilities in nuclei resulting from alpha-induced reactions on light targets.  Specifically, this review delves into detailed assessments of energy levels in 12C, 16O, and 20Ne nuclei, which have been studied through various reactions including direct reactions, transfer reactions, and reactions that produce neutron-rich or neutron-deficient nuclei.  As a methodology, this review employs a combinatorial algorithm to extract excited energy spectra and their corresponding properties from a vast dataset generated from gamma-ray angular distribution and spectroscopy analysis.  This approach allows us to update existing energy level bases and transition probabilities for a range of collective states in the mentioned targets.  Furthermore, this review discusses approaches to solving the density matrix, which is essential for extracting transition probabilities from cross-section data, and presents two methods: a direct approach and an indirect approach via a generalized sum rule.

These computational results provide new insights into the geometric object known as the Hessian, which is associated with a smooth cubic curve. Moreover, it allows us to display the Hessian's symmetry more easily.

the characteristics of nuclear structure and dynamics, can be investigated through various experiments utilizing relativistic heavy-ion collisions.  The freeze-out density, at which particles stop evolving on average, is an essential factor influencing the interpretation of experiments.  Due to fluctuations in fluctuations, the freeze-out density distribution cannot be determined with certainty.  Monte Carlo generators, used to describe experiments and analyze data, need to be trained on a large set of freeze-out density data.  However, current training sets are limited, restricting our ability to accurately describe experiments and derive reliable conclusions.  In this study, we investigate the characteristics of freeze-out density in an extended way, preparing a large set of 700k events for training purposes.  Using this set, we investigate limitations and potential biases affecting the description of experiments.  Specifically, we examine how to accurately describe experiments when training is done on a limited set of events, and derive reliable conclusions from experiments.  Our findings provide guidelines for ensuring the accurate description of experiments and reliable conclusions in experiments.

the continuum problem is consistent with specific theories that include $\mathsf{ZFC}$, and we demonstrate this using a novel approach focusing on the principles related to the power of the continuum.  Our analysis reveals that the power of the continuum can be anywhere within a specific range defined by two cardinalities, and we refer to this range as $\Theta$.  We then identify two distinct set theoretical hypotheses, one that results in the continuum having the smallest possible cardinality within $\Theta$, and another that leads to the largest possible cardinality, both of which are consistent with $\mathsf{ZFC}$.  Furthermore, we establish that the continuum problem may hold true for certain finite ordinal indices, and to achieve this, we develop a new type of continuous function.  This function allows us to formulate a specific transfinite equation that defines the $\Psi_\alpha$ functions, and we prove that the values of these functions, along with their derivatives, are countable for all positive integers $\alpha$.  We also demonstrate the application of our new continuous function to the power of the continuum by showing that any standard model that satisfies the continuum hypothesis has a specific property, and we utilize this property to define a specific $\Psi_\alpha$ function whose value at that ordinal is the continuum, and all the values of which, along with its derivatives, are countable.

We clarify that radiantly induced symmetry breaking can occur while meeting the requirements of the MSSSM in both its electroweak and GUT forms.  We calculate the radiance-driven forces behind symmetry breaking in both theories and demonstrate that the radiance-driven four-dimensional gauge symmetry breaking occurs at an energy scale higher than $10^{10}$ GeV in the MSSSM, which is beyond the current age of the universe.  We also determine the minimum value for the Planck constant that would allow for both radiantly induced symmetry breaking in the MSSSM and the emergence of the cosmologically relevant axion-like particles predicted by the model. Marriage problem is defined as a set of distinct women $W$, a set of distinct men $M$, and a compatibility relation $R$ specifying each person's preferred matches.  The problem of determining the most unstable aspect, or the smallest number of broken preferences, occurs when a matching can be found that doesn't result in any individuals disapproving of their assigned partner.  This problem has been previously studied in a restricted form, known as the Ham Sandwich Theorem, which states that given three subsets of people, with each person belonging to one of the subsets, there will always exist a middle layer that intersects with all three subsets.  By applying this same concept to the Stable Marriage problem, there will exist a middle layer that intersects with the largest and smallest unstable aspects.  This paper also provides multiple new upper bounds for certain variants of the Stable Marriage problem, specifically the average and worst-case case bounds for the largest unstable aspect, and the worst-case bound for the second largest unstable aspect.  These new bounds offer significant improvements over previously known limits, which were largely unclear due to the problems' high computational complexity.

  exact star models, researchers can determine the birth star's type.  Since

the Higgs mechanism, physicists have been searching for an understanding of why the electroweak symmetry was broken.  Within the past fifteen years, researchers have proposed numerous theories attempting to address this question, often involving extra dimensions that prevent certain particles from accessing certain areas.  By re-examining the properties of braneworld scenarios, particularly in scenarios with our universe being closely linked to one extra dimension, we have discovered that certain problems with symmetry breaking can be resolved without encountering any conflicts with recent astrophysics findings.  Specifically, we show that in 5D models with a background brane where the Higgs mechanism occurs, a certain type of instability associated with the GUT Higgs mechanism can be prevented if the threshold energy for accessibility is higher than that of the other particles by at least forty orders of magnitude.  We also find that in 6D models with two asymmetric extra dimensions, the threshold energy for accessibility can be controlled by the energy of the other particles, making it possible for the Higgs mechanism to occur without any issues with symmetry breaking.  Moreover, we determine that in all these models, the amount of symmetry breaking is directly proportional to the curvature of the branes.

To model extreme value behavior, a theoretical framework is established using high-probability bounds, and the model's parameters are shown to have the desired asymptotic properties. Notably, no specific distribution assumptions are made about the underlying data. Instead, dependence within the data is accounted for through the use of a particular rate condition. A recent development in statistical analysis, the extreme value framework is accompanied by an overview of existing literature. Estimation of extreme value quantiles through regression has been previously explored using specific data distributions, but this work appears to be the first such study to relax those assumptions. Two key results are presented in this paper. First, bounds are derived for the difference between a quantile regression estimator and the true extreme value quantile. These bounds converge as the sample size increases, with the rate of convergence influenced by a variance condition. Secondly, an extreme value framework is established for the difference between a quantile regression estimator and the corresponding population quantile. This difference is shown to converge at a rate influenced by a specific rate condition. These results are accompanied by an overview of existing literature on extreme value theory and quantile regression.

A particular variant of this model features a non-canonical scalar field and a potential that is both complex and slowly varying.  When rolling down this potential, the scalar field experiences a symmetry breaking, which leads to a particular pattern of particle formation.  A key aspect of this process is the formation of adiabatic waterfalls, which occur when the scalar field's real part transitions into a non-adiabatic regime while the complex part continues to roll down the potential.  A more intricate phenomenon is the multi-waterfall process, which could result in the formation of dark matter.  This concept has been represented mathematically and compared to observational constraints from cosmic microwave background, which indicate that the inflation duration must have been around 6.3 digits of e-foldings.  Fortunately, the multi-waterfall process does not produce any primordial fluctuations that could conflict with observations.  Furthermore, this model predicts the consistency of matter and radiation temperatures during the cosmic microwave background analysis.  It also predicts the amplitude of primordial fluctuations to be around 2.35, which aligns with observations, and the specific pattern of fluctuations known as the 'local type', which is consistent with 98% of observations.

Furthermore, researchers are interested in using the memory effect to infer the equation of state, especially when the merger produces a neutron star remnant. Initially, studies have examined this phenomenon using analytical approaches and simplified models. In our research, we utilize a vast array of realistic neutron star mergers generated through numerical simulations, represented by the LORENNI waveforms, which are characterized by 718 different equations of state. By extracting the memory effect from these waveforms, we calculate the root-mean-square values for distinct binary neutron star mergers and their corresponding remnant stars. Interestingly, we discover that the memory effect exhibits a binary-remnant distinction of approximately 0.36, independent of the initial binary parameters, which can be broken down into binary-remnant distinctions of about 0.26 due to the remnant's mass and angular momentum, when considering all possible neutron star remnant masses between 1.4 and 2.0 solar masses. Additionally, we find that the memory effect can be distinguished based on the remnant's angular momentum at approximately 0.05 solar angular momentum units, which further solidifies the feasibility of employing the memory effect to infer the equation of state from neutron star mergers through gravitational wave observations.

In this study, we explore an alternative, seemingly unlikely aspect of ULAs, namely their interaction with large-scale cosmic web structures.  Assuming that the vacuum average of a ULA field's amplitude is proportional to its local overdensity, we develop a model which links this phenomenon to the amplification of ULA oscillations and, as a result, modifies the AMOM signal.  By analyzing this new interaction within the framework of the 21cmFAST semi-analytical simulation of the cosmic web, we find that it could mitigate the discord between AMOM observations and ULA predictions for their interaction with photons.  However, this new model still faces a conflict with asteroseismology constraints on ULA masses.  We also discovered that our new model exclusively addresses the 0.1-10 $\mu$K amplitude range of the AMOM anomaly, whereas all other interactions fall outside the currently valid constraints of $\sim$ 1 eV scale.  Furthermore, we found that the AMOM data alone are insufficient to provide exhaustive ULA parameter bounds.  Lastly, we project that upcoming cosmic web density maps from the Euclid satellite, combined with AMOM data, may pave the way for ULA mass range discoveries as early as 2030.

To coordinate and standardize these methods, a comprehensive framework, called Meta-ATG, has been developed, featuring a suite of state-of-the-art test case generation techniques. black hole binary mergers in Kerr spacetimes, specifically influencing the radiation patterns of gravitational waves, are investigated in this research.  This study compares the reference solutions for binary mergers involving spinning black holes in Kerr orbits around a supermassive black hole, focusing on non-rotating black holes with masses much larger than their companion objects.  The analysis leverages quasi-equivalent waveforms to determine changes in gravitational wave patterns caused by spinning black holes with masses much smaller than their Kerr counterparts.  The findings indicate that spin influences the radiation patterns of gravitational waves in binary black hole mergers, particularly visible in the amplitude modulation effect produced by the spin.  The impact of spin on the meridional angular distribution of the gravitational wave energy release is particularly significant at low frequencies, and it persists even after the binary black hole system approaches its merger point.  The results also show that the spin influence leads to an asymmetry in the gravitational wave radiation pattern, producing more intense waves on the side of the orbit opposite to the direction of the spinning black hole's precessional motion.  The amplitude of this effect is found to be a function of the angular momentum of the spinning black hole, and it correlates with the degree of precession experienced by the binary black hole system prior to its merger.

These paths contain a sequence of points in the manifold's boundary, along with their corresponding local charts, along with a set of vectors in the tangent space, along with an interval of the real line.  The points in the sequence are required to have the same coordinate system, the vectors in the tangent space are required to be part of a set known as the tangent space's exterior product, and the interval of the real line is required to be part of a set known as the r-torus.  We then define a set known as the set of graded contact elements as the intersection of the set of graded vertical paths and the set known as the contact distribution.  We then use this definition to establish a relationship between the set of graded contact elements and a set known as the set of graded symplectic forms.  We then use this relationship to demonstrate that the set of graded symplectic forms is equivalent to a set known as the set of strongly non-degenerate 2-forms.  We then use this equivalence to demonstrate that the set of graded symplectic forms is in a one-to-one correspondence with a set known as the set of strongly non-degenerate 2-forms. assessing the reliability of weather forecasts and global climate models.  Despite advancements in ensemble techniques, predicting extreme weather events remains a significant challenge.  A deeper understanding of ensemble performance is critical in this regard.  This study employs 10-year datasets from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Ensemble Prediction System (ECMWF EPS) to examine the characteristics of ensemble forecasts in predicting tropical cyclone tracks.  Specifically, we investigate the spread and member bias of the ensemble forecast ensemble.  Our findings reveal that the ensemble spread is significantly correlated with the distance to the forecast point, whereas the correlation with the wind field plays a lesser role.  Our results also indicate that certain ensemble members exhibit persistent bias in forecasting tropical cyclone tracks.  We further develop a weighted ensemble forecast method, giving greater weight to the ensemble members that are less biased.  When applied to forecasting tropical cyclone tracks, our results indicate that this method yields a higher correlation coefficient of 0.89, compared to the control group with a correlation coefficient of 0.76.  Our study provides valuable insights into the characteristics of ensemble forecasts in predicting tropical cyclone tracks.  Our proposed method can be used to improve the accuracy of ensemble forecast methods.

non-perfect graph G and an integer k greater than zero: given that the edge set of G can be partitioned into k disjoint subsets, what conditions must these subsets meet in order for the perfect graph H, which results from G's edges being colored with these subsets, to have a maximum clique number no greater than r? 

  A relation, denoted as k-r, is defined between the set of these partitions and the integer r, where it represents the smallest number required for any collection of these partitions to satisfy the condition mentioned above for a given subgraph of G, which contains no more than r vertices.

quark mass has sparked interest in the $W$ boson mass determination from
lattice QCD. A major complication in this process is the top quark's rapid
decay, which makes it impossible to measure the $W \to t\bar t$ process directly.
 
A commonly employed method to overcome this challenge involves lattice
simulations of the $W$ boson decay into light quarks, with the top quark mass
being a non-perturbative parameter. Given the uncertainty in the $W$ boson
mass, a lattice simulation of the $W \to u d$ decay width seems a reliable
approach to estimate the $W$ boson mass. This study involves multiple
lattice simulations, with different configurations aimed at determining the $W$
boson mass based on the $W \to u d$ decay width. The top quark mass was set
at 160 GeV, while the $W$ boson mass was determined to be approximately
80.6 GeV, with a corresponding $W \to u d$ decay width of 1.49 ns$^{-1}$.

To tackle this issue, we have developed ML-Sync, a unification framework that enables ML model deployment across different computing platforms. These platforms include edge devices, such as those based on OpenWRT, Linux, and mobile operating systems, as well as cloud services, such as TensorFlow (TF) and Microsoft Machine Learning (MLL). have excelled in various graph-based applications,   but their success is hindered by the lack of suitable evaluation metrics.  A fair GNN evaluation requires considering both performance and issues with the data representation resulting from the network.  Current evaluation approaches for GNNs are limited and don't cover all crucial aspects.  We believe a comprehensive evaluation of GNNs should involve existing classification benchmarks, as well as novel metrics addressing the embedded node features, such as topological properties and spatial relationships.  These features are inherently tied to the graph structure and are often disregarded in traditional evaluation frameworks.  To address this, we introduce PyDME, a unified testing environment that enables the evaluation of GNNs in various graph classification settings, including novel metrics focused on the embedded node features.  Key advantages of PyDME include its support for custom datasets and an extensive range of benchmark GNN models.  We showcase the efficacy of PyDME through an in-depth analysis of graph classification tasks, highlighting the robustness of 14 widely-used GNN models.  These experiments reveal that GNN model choices significantly influence classification performance and often result in subpar data representations.  Furthermore, our findings indicate that GNNs tend to struggle with topological properties and spatial relationships.  We believe PyDME will serve as a valuable resource for both researchers and practitioners to explore the intricate relationship between GNNs, their internal workings, and the graphs upon which they operate.

XNCL constrains models to adhere to prior knowledge represented by a set, defined through functional equations, which facilitates interpretation and prediction. By incorporating differential privacy, XNCL's ability to learn is ensured while limiting the impact of sensitive data. We demonstrate that Privacy-Preserving XNCL (PP-XNCL) maintains the same optimization efficiency as conventional XNCL by overcoming the significant learning barrier associated with privacy. Specifically, PP-XNCL achieves the same convergence rate as conventional XNCL despite privacy constraints. Additionally, we establish an optimal privacy loss bound for PP-XNCL in the most general case and derive a useful consequence for XNCL with a specific type of constraint. Furthermore, we provide an easily implementable privacy-preserving algorithm based on local differential privacy. Finally, our extensive numerical results highlight the outstanding performance of PP-XNCL.

introduction to the field of study focusing on the interconnection between the Frobenius map and geometric Langlands correspondence, an area of research that has only begun to be explored in recent years. Key concepts, including the Frobenius map, geometric Langlands correspondence, Satake correspondence, and constructible etale sheaf theory, are reviewed in this presentation. Some newly developed results, such as the description of the image of the geometric Langlands functoriality map after applying the Frobenius map, are also highlighted. The relationship between the Frobenius map and geometric Langlands correspondence can be seen as a combination of two main developments in mathematics. The first of these involves the description of the image of the geometric Langlands functoriality map after applying the Frobenius map, which can also be described using representations in $p$-adic groups by applying the Satake correspondence. The second of these involves the description of the image of the Satake correspondence equipped with the action of Hecke operators, which was known as the hardest part to determine. This result provides a powerful tool that can be used to establish the applications of the geometric Langlands correspondence in characteristic $p$.

Despite its benefits, the conventional VOF technique often experiences difficulties in resolving interfaces that are steep.  To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel VOF method that utilizes a hierarchical mesh framework to track interfaces across multiple levels of refinement.  By doing so, our method accurately captures the sharp boundaries of interfaces even within coarse-mesh simulations.  Unlike other interface-c Capturing methods, our approach does not introduce artificial thicknesses associated with broadening interfaces.  Instead, our method leverages the broadening parameter (δ) native to conventional VOF, although its influence is minimized as the method resolves sharp interfaces.  We have mathematically analyzed the error of our method relative to traditional VOF, demonstrating that our approach offers a linear improvement over the original VOF method.  We have tested our method against a range of benchmark tests, including a rotating corner sink and a breaking dam scenario, and found it to provide more accurate results than the conventional VOF technique.  Specifically, our results indicate that our method reduces the error caused by resolving interfaces on coarse meshes from O(ε^(-1)) to a more manageable O(ε^(-1)/δ).  We have also validated our method using a refined mesh, eliminating the artificial broadening parameter (δ), and observed a further reduction in the overall error to O(ε^(-1)).

This self-modulation occurs when there is an interplay between the positive dispersion of high-density waves and the negative dispersion of low-density waves. We analyze this effect within a general framework that accounts for both acoustic and non-acoustic modes. We observe that the positive dispersion of high-density waves results from the interaction between particles during collisions, which can be understood by considering a simplified Hertz contact model. We find that the ratio of densities between adjacent wave crests or troughs increases exponentially over time, with the rate of this increase determined by the frequency of the wave and a dimensionless parameter that measures the degree of non-linearity. This increase in density amplifies the force of gravity between particles, eventually limiting the growth of waves through a process that could be visible in experiments.

This study experimentally examined the influence of Marangoni numbers on droplet evaporation, with contact angles measured over time for droplets of glycerin and water on polystyrene substrates of varying surface energies.  It was observed that even at relatively low Marongani numbers, where gravity's influence dominates, the evaporation rate is accelerated due to Marangoni's impact.  A theoretical model was developed to analyze this phenomenon, revealing that the evaporation front's asymmetry plays a significant role.  As the Marangoni number increases, the droplet's outer layer evaporates more quickly, consistent with observations.  Furthermore, it was found that the Kapitzin mechanism, where the surface tension gradient drives the mixture from the warmer center to the cooler periphery, predominately operates at high Marangoni numbers; whereas, at lower numbers, the mechanism reverses, aligning with Levich's analysis.  This research provides new insights into the complex interplay of forces governing droplet evaporation.

embedding field asks for the maximum number of planar embeddings a graph can have, considering all possible orientations of its edges. This question was previously answered for bipartite graphs by Courcans' theorem, which stated that a bipartite graph has at most 2n-2 planar embeddings, with n being the number of vertices. However, this upper limit was shown to be reached by multiple examples, leading researchers to seek the minimum number required for some graphs. Recently, a new family of bipartite graphs was found, achieving at least 2n-1 planar embeddings in some cases, proving the original theorem of Courcans correct. The original theorem stated that a bipartite graph with n vertices has at most 2n-1 planar embeddings, but this new family of graphs shows this limit is reached when the graph is a complete bipartite graph, which was not clear before.

Converting a DNN into an equivalent Formal Neural Network (FNN) has been proposed as a viable method for doing so.  We offer the first-ever FNN specification framework that provides a precise definition for FNNs and a set of formal specifications they can adhere to.  Our proposed approach to creating FNNs involves a novel transformation process, starting from the input DNN, which generates an equivalent FNN along with a formal specification.  We have developed a prototype system that includes a FNN translator tool, supported by a mathematical proof, to guarantee the equivalence between the original DNN and the generated FNN.  What's more, we have also derived a method for deriving a formal specification for the FNN, which can be utilized for hybrid symbolic-concrete counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CGAR) abstractions to enhance the precision of the FNN.  We have tested our approach with a benchmark dataset consisting of 13 diverse DNN models across five different categories, which showed promising results in terms of accuracy, robustness, and CGAR refinement levels.

  serves as an indicator of mass loss through stellar winds.  Mass loss rates of these 
  winds are often estimated through empirical relations tied to stellar parameters such 
  as X-ray luminosity, spectral type, or convection zone depth.  However, there has been 
  limited research on the relationship between X-ray luminosity and mass loss rates in 
  these stars.  To address this, we analyzed high-resolution spectral observations to 
  determine mass loss rates in 23 active G-K stars using iron absorption features, 
  also accessing X-ray flux data for these stars.  Our results indicate mass loss rates 
  are linearly proportional to X-ray luminosity as well as wind outflow velocities. 
  Specifically, mass loss rates increase with increasing X-ray luminosity by 1.46 solar 
  mass per year for every 10^(-3) erg/s/cm^2 increase, and similarly, they rise by 
  3.8 solar mass per year for every km/s increase in wind velocity.  These findings 
  provide a new set of relations useful for estimating mass loss rates in these stars 
  based on their X-ray properties and wind characteristics.

These games have an inherent symmetry that allows them to be reduced to a lower-dimensional representation, specifically the number of states. However, the movement of these fractures is complex and requires further study.  We have developed a computational model that incorporates fluid-driven fracture propagation, mapping it onto a two-dimensional surface within a three-dimensional space.  By linking fracture propagation to fluid flow, this model solves the mixed problem of fracture growth and fluid movement.  Using this model, we have simulated fracture growth in different types of rocks and observed that our results accurately match previous theoretical predictions.  Furthermore, we have used our model to study the movement of fractures over various scales, from centimeters to kilometers, and found that the results align with our current understanding of fracture growth.  Additionally, this model enables us to determine how the composition of rocks affects fracture growth and, in some cases, provides evidence that fractures grow more evenly.  Finally, this model has the capability to be combined with other computational models to analyze co-flows and also can be adapted to various types of fractures.

aviolet threshold behavior in quantum field theories using quantum mechanical analogues. A specific focus is on describing the characteristic patterns of UV divergences, finite-size effects, and Regge trajectories within these systems. A well-known set of conformally symmetric spacetimes, the Brinkmann spaces, serves as our primary quantum mechanical framework. Notably, the Schr\"{o}dinger picture of bound state formation through scattering can be applied to these spacetimes, yielding insights into the emergence of UV singularities, such as Landau poles, and the characteristics of Regge trajectories, including the linear relationship of spin to energy. A key finding is that the interplay between the conformal symmetry of spacetimes and the Wightman axioms for quantum states reveals that the UV threshold in quantum field theories corresponds to a light cone within the scattering matrix, across which the Borel summand transitions from analytic to non-analytic. This understanding is confirmed through both perturbative calculations and studies of non-perturbative properties of the systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the UV threshold also defines the boundary between stable and unstable bound states. Additionally, we explore how changes in the background geometry affect the UV divergences and threshold behavior. A key observation made in this work has been independently confirmed by a separate analysis.

To address this lack of research, we propose the ListGenerator, a novel dataset consisting of both plain text and table formats generated independently by different methods.  Our dataset comprises 200,000 examples of generated text, covering five domains, and introduces the task of Conditional Generation with Format Consistency (CGFC), which demands generated text to match a predetermined format while still making sense semantically.  To effectively handle CGFC, we introduce the ListGenerator RNN, a model capable of processing both sequential text and concurrent structure information. learning, data collection, assumes knowledge of the distribution from which data samples are drawn.  However, when learning from limited and biased datasets as is common in many real-world settings, relying solely on these methods can be unwise.  What is needed instead is a way to generalize from these imperfect datasets.  This challenge is particularly acute in meta-learning where the primary goal is to generalize to new tasks.  Notably, recent meta-learning algorithms like MEMO and PROMP that focus on robust generalization during the meta-training phase have been specifically designed to address this issue.  These algorithms deliberately introduce noise into the training process with the aim of developing a more robust task learner that generalizes effectively to new, unseen tasks.  What is needed now is a theoretical framework that underpins their success.  Our proposed framework, titled Generalized Trainability, provides a clear explanation for why these algorithms are able to generalize more effectively.  It frames the problem in terms of the relationship between the training and inference phases and identifies the concept of generalized trainability as the key to successful generalization.  Our proposed framework also sheds light on the specific design choices that contribute to the successful generalization observed with these algorithms.  Ultimately, it facilitates the development of new algorithms that leverage the idea of generalized trainability to achieve robust generalization performance.

the use of conformal mapping in solving boundary value problems for analytic functions. Key topics covered include the application of conformal mapping to solve Dirichlet problems, the development of quasiconformal mapping techniques, and the demonstration of the solvability of Dirichlet problems through conformal mapping. We also examine the connection between the Schauder estimate and the use of conformal mapping in solving specific boundary value problems. A notable section delves into the history of the Dirichlet problem's solvability in the plane, highlighting important contributions from Grange, Bellet, and Lehto. Additionally, we explore the impact of conformal mapping on the study of boundary properties of meromorphic functions. A notable result, the Proofs of Theorems 1 and 2, is a direct adaptation of arguments initially presented by Lehto in his 1981 paper "Boundary behavior of meromorphic functions".

used to measure the relationship between ranked data sets.  This study examines the test's effectiveness when dealing with partially ranked data sets.  We created artificial data sets that were partially ranked by random order, and analyzed how the test's results compare to the actual correlations within these data sets.  Our findings show that the test tends to overestimate the strength of the correlation as the number of partially ranked items increases.  Additionally, we discovered that the test's accuracy improves when the rankings within each data set become more consistent in reflecting a particular correlation.  Our research suggests that relying solely on the test may lead to inaccurate conclusions when dealing with partially ranked data sets of sufficient depth, and that other methods such as information theory may offer more reliable measures of correlation in these situations.

Based on a proposed node location distribution model, we develop a novel Information Collection Surface (ICS) to evaluate and compare the efficiency of various point collection strategies. challenge in genetics.  A key aspect of functional genomics involves identifying regions of high epigenetic density which are linked to specific functional roles.  Recent studies utilizing Encode data have shed light on how regions with high epigenetic markings are Enriched for specific functions by creating profiles known as epigenomic maps.  These profiles are created by combining regions with similar epigenetic patterns to reveal underlying structures of the genetic code.  A method known as MultiTask Graph AutoEncoders (MT-GAE) is proposed which is an innovative technique for building epigenomic maps from scratch without relying on pre-trained models.  MT-GAE is a graph neural network model designed for latent structure learning and positional encoding learning by simultaneously handling multi-task regression and graph structural learning.  Experimental results show MT-GAE outperforms current state-of-the-art models in constructing epigenomic maps and demonstrates its versatility in multiple organisms and tissues.  Furthermore, MT-GAE is capable of reversing the encoding process to obtain specific functional enrichments from general epigenetic patterns.  By applying MT-GAE to biological data from Encode, valuable insights are gained on the structural relationship between different functional roles and the corresponding epigenetic patterns that define them.

Using an appropriate perturbation approach suitable for small values of the ratio of the rotation rate to the wave frequency, we examine how the shape of the wave packet influences the development of zonal flows.  We find that in regions where the wave frequency is much greater than the rotation rate, the development of a uniform distribution of phases, indicative of an inertial wave packet, is accompanied by a roughly preserved spatial structure.  Conversely, in areas where the rotation rate significantly exceeds the wave frequency, a marked disparity arises between the inner region of the wave packet, characterized by an approximately uniform distribution of phases and marked vortex-street formation, and the outer region, marked by a significant disparity in phase values and the emergence of a vortex ring.  We connect our findings to recent experimental observations in rotating Bose-Einstein condensates and predict similar phenomena to occur in other systems characterized by invariant structures, such as dark rings in rotating photorefractive crystals.

This logic, called LTL(POLY), utilizes constraints from polyomino shapes to define sets of paths that can be reached within specific graph configurations. A key aspect of analyzing LTL(POLY) involves considering its relationship to constraints defined by polyomino shapes. These shape constraints can be analyzed by referring to equivalent, simpler patterns known as tilings. An important concept in tilings is their recognition, with known algorithms for determining whether a set of start configurations can lead to a specific final arrangement. However, there are tilings whose start configurations cannot be determined. We explore the complexity of deciding whether a set of start configurations can lead to any arrangement at all. This decision-making process is complex for general graphs, but if the graph is a line, the complexity is reduced. Additionally, determining whether a set of start configurations can lead to multiple different arrangements is also complex for general graphs, but if the graph is a line, the complexity is reduced.

Advances in machine learning, such as robust regression and neural network-based alternatives like NNIT, are exploring ways to analyze data with significant outliers. These methods assume that data follows a normal distribution; however, real-world data often follows a non-normal distribution, as identified in the BDCA dataset. Successfully deploying these methods in practice requires verifying their performance across diverse data sets. This paper contributes to this effort by evaluating NNIT on data sets with artificially introduced outliers, having a significantly broader range of 50 times that of the original data, under various conditions. Results show that NNIT accurately predicts targets within a range of 0.1 to 1.1 times the deviation of the data set's variation, demonstrating that NNIT's performance is unaffected by outliers when the data set is balanced. We establish the result that the set of paths that are accessible within a certain time interval contains a subset that can be approximated by a line.
